extracted.intended_audience: regulatory commenters, public-interest advocates, and attorneys preparing notice-and-comment submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting public comments on proposed administrative rules that use procedural arguments to expose deviations from statutory intent, supply oversight ammunition, reduce information asymmetries, and document procedural defects that enable political or judicial pushback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite statutory purpose and identify intended beneficiary class
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment cite the statutory purpose and identify the intended beneficiary class?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke the original statutory bargain: who was Congress trying to help? Explain how the proposed rule departs from that intent. Use the statute's purpose language and legislative history where helpful to show misalignment between the rule and the class the statute was meant to protect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose information the agency has not disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment expose information the agency has not disclosed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand specific data, challenge agency assumptions, and identify gaps in the record. Convert private agency information into public information by pointing out missing studies, undisclosed analyses, or facts omitted from the rulemaking record. Provide citations, alternative data sources, or specific requests for documents/studies to fill information asymmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide ammunition for congressional oversight (specific harms, costs, affected districts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment provide ammunition for congressional oversight by identifying specific harms, costs, and affected constituencies or districts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly flag deviations from statutory intent, identify who will be harmed, and provide documentation (e.g., quantified costs, affected districts, employer/worker impacts) that Congress or oversight actors could use as 'fire-alarm' evidence. Tailor facts to the interests of likely oversight players and show concrete consequences rather than abstract objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document procedural failings in the rulemaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment document a procedural failing (inadequate alternatives, missing data, truncated comment period)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify procedural deficiencies—such as inadequate notice, undisclosed studies, truncated comment periods, failure to consider reasonable alternatives—that raise costs for agencies attempting to favor unintended beneficiaries. Explain how procedural lapses create grounds for political pressure or judicial challenge and provide concrete examples or timelines showing the deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect the rule to the political coalition that enacted the underlying statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment connect the rule to the political coalition that enacted the underlying statute (e.g., labor for OSHA rules, environmentalists for CAA rules)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the rule affects or departs from the interests of the coalition that supported the original statute. Use sector- or coalition-specific examples (e.g., labor, environmental groups) to demonstrate that the rule stacks the deck toward unintended beneficiaries and thus undermines the statutory bargain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize procedural arguments even when filing substantive objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment emphasize procedural defects as a strategic lever even if the commenter also raises substantive objections?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McNollgast warns that novice commenters often underweight procedural arguments while repeat players exploit them. Even substantive commenters should flag procedural defects (missing analyses, truncated timelines, flawed notice) because procedural claims can attract political oversight and are often more actionable than purely substantive complaints. Encourage documenting procedural issues alongside policy critiques.
